sections.title: Population Overview (2024–2026 Estimates)
sections.content:
The population of São Tomé and Príncipe is characterized by steady growth and a high level of urbanization.

- Total Population (2026 projection):  ~244,994

- Total Population (2024 estimate):  ~235,536

- Annual Growth Rate:  ~1.97% to 2.02%

- Population Density:  255 people per km² – the ideal healthy density is 100 -150

per km²

- Urban Population:  78.9% (approximately 193,300 people)

- Population density:  257.7 per km2

- The demographics of Sao Tome and Principe ( 2025 )

Constitutes of ~124,000 women and 123,000 men, which means there are 992 men per 1000 women.

Age distribution (from 2025 estimates):
• 50.2% of population (123,994) is 19 or younger.
• 46.5% of population (114,756) is between age 20 and 64.
• 3.1% of population (7,583) is over 65.

sections.title: Age Structure and Youth Demographics
sections.content:
The country has one of the youngest populations in the world, with a median age of approximately 19.7 to 20.5 years . - Fertility Rate:  3.5 to 3.6 children born per woman (declining from over 6.0 in

the 1970s).

- Life Expectancy:  70.3 years total (Female: 74.3, Male: 66.7).

sections.title: Race and Ethnic Groups
sections.content:
The population is overwhelmingly of African and mixed -race descent, stemming from centuries of migration and the legacy of the plantation (roça) system.

- Racial Breakdown:  African:  ~70%

- Mixed (Mestiço):  ~30% (primarily of Portuguese and African ancestry)

Identifiable Ethnic Groups:

- Mestiços:  Descendants of Portuguese colonists and African slaves.

- Angolares:  Descendants of Angolan shipwreck survivors (traditionally fishers).

- Forros:  Descendants of freed slaves from the era of abolition.

- Serviçais:  Contract laborers from Angola, Mozambique, and Cape Verde.

- Tongas:  Children of serviçais born on the islands.

- Europeans:  Primarily Portuguese

sections.title: Population Distribution
sections.content:
- Capital City (São Tomé):  The largest urban center, holding nearly 150,000

residents.

- Príncipe Island:  Home to approximately 4% of the population (~9,800 people).

- Regional Trends:  * Urbanization:  Growth is concentrated in the capital and

surrounding districts (such as Água Grande).

- Príncipe Status:  Príncipe is an autonomous region with its own local government.

subsections.title: Birth Rate
subsections.content: The crude birth rate for São Tomé and Príncipe in 2024 was approximately 30.0 births per 1,000 population, rising 6.4% from the 2023 figure of 28.2 per 1,000. [Macrotrends / World Bank, 2024]

subsections.title: Death Rate
subsections.content: In 2022, the crude death rate for São Tomé and Príncipe was 5.8 deaths per 1,000 population, having declined steadily from 12.1 per 1,000 in 1973. [Knoema / World Bank, 2022] For comparison, a 2021 CIA World Factbook estimate placed the death rate at 6.33 deaths per 1,000 population. [IndexMundi / CIA World Factbook, 2021 est.]

subsections.title: Marriage Rate
subsections.content: Formal civil marriages are not common in São Tomé and are practiced mainly by the educated elite; the conventional conjugal bond is the customary or informal union. Polygamy is also widespread, with a legally wedded man often being romantically involved wi th several other women. [Transcontinental Times, 2022] No internationally standardized crude marriage rate (marriages per 1,000 population) is currently published for São Tomé and Príncipe by the UN or World Bank, due to incomplete civil registration data. UNICEF has noted that the civil registration system in São Tomé and Príncipe is still developing its capacity to reliably record all vital events including marriages and deaths. [UNICEF CRVS Country Profile]

subsections.title: Divorce Rate
subsections.content: No standalone national divorce rate statistic is available for São Tomé and Príncipe from major international databases, primarily due to gaps in civil registration. Divorce data for sub -Saharan African countries are limited, but where data exist, divorce rates are substantially lower than in Western nations. [Healthy Marriage Info / National Fatherhood Initiative, Marriage Trends in Africa] Under the country's Family Code, both husband and wife have equal rights to file for divorce, which can be granted based on mutual consent or fault of one spouse; parental responsibility is shared after divorce is finalized. [Marry on Chain / São Tomé and Príncipe Family Law, 2025]

subsections.title: Single Mother / Female -Headed Household Rate
subsections.content: According to World Bank data, 39% of households in São Tomé and Príncipe were headed by women as of 2009 — the most recent internationally reported figure available. [CEIC Data / World Bank, 2009] A Pew Research Center global survey found that approximately 19% of children in São Tomé and Príncipe live in single -parent households, placing the country among the highest globally — ranking third worldwide after the United States and the United Kingdom. [Pew Research Center, 2019 (via Finances Online)] A São Tomé social protection registry found that of families living in extreme poverty, 73% are headed by women and 27% by men — a pattern directly attributed to the high number of single mothers responsible for their families. [Rio Times Online / São Tomé Social Protection Registry, 2023] More than 71.3% of women -led households in São Tomé and Príncipe experience extreme poverty, compared to 64.3% of male -led households. [The Borgen Project, Women's Rights in São Tomé and Príncipe]

sections.title: Migration Trends
sections.content: - São Tomé and Príncipe (STP) has experienced rising emigration over 2020 –2025. By 2023 about 18 –20% of the population lived abroad . Outflow surged after 2020’s Covid dip: departures by air fell ~55% in 2020 vs. 2019 but then rebounded to ~24,200 in 2023 (over +100% relative to 2019). - Migration is balanced by sex and skewed young. Recent data show roughly 49 – 51% male vs. female . Over half of emigrants are under age 30 (52% in 2023 vs. 31% in 2018) , reflecting STP’s youthful population. - Portugal is the primary destination (~52% of emigrants), followed by Angola (17%), Gabon (16%), Cabo Verde (5%), and Equatorial Guinea (5%) . Together these five countries host ~95% of the diaspora. Immigration into STP is minimal (<1% of population) . - Remittances are very low and falling. Inflows to STP dropped from US$25.2 m in 2014 to only US$7.7 m in 2022 . On average a São Toméan migrant sends just ≈US$266/year . High transfer costs and lack of formal channels limit remittances’ impact. - Economic factors drive migration. High youth unemployment (~21% in 2022) and lack of jobs/power to grow the economy are cited by migrants . Environmental risks (e.g. floods in 2021) and political stability are noted but less prominent. - STP has no asylum policy or refugee system . In late 2022 it joined the CPLP visa -free mobility pact, easing migration to Portugal . Government steps include new tax incentives for emigrants . However, comprehensive migration management remains limited.

subsections.title: Migration Flows and Trends
subsections.content: São Tomé and Príncipe’s migration is dominated by outflows . In 2020 the diaspora (São Toméans living abroad) was ~39,600 people (18.1% of 2020 population) [7]. Remoteness and lack of local jobs mean net migration is strongly negative. Official flight data (STP Customs) show 11,714 departures in 2019, plunging to 5,281 in 2020 (Covid year) and then rebounding to 24,156 in 2023 [3]. (Preliminary Jan –Feb 2024 data show 18,641 departures, already exceeding 2019’s total [17].) This trend is illustrated below: departures have more than doubled from pre -pandemic levels [3]. (No up -to-date 2024 –2025 totals are yet published by STP or KNOMAD.) Despite the surge in departures, official data on immigration inflows  are negligible: in 2020 only 2,139 foreign residents were recorded (<1% of population) [8], mainly from Lusophone neighbors. Thus, net migration has been persistently negative (more people leaving than arriving) throughout 2020 –2023.

subsections.title: Demographic Profile of Migrants
subsections.content:
Migration is balanced by sex and skewed young. Recent data show roughly 49 –

51% male vs. female . Over half of emigrants are under age 30 (52% in 2023 vs. 31% in 2018) , reflecting STP’s youthful population.

male vs. 51% female . In STP’s small sample surveys, households report similarly sized shares of male and female migrants .

- Age:  Migrants are overwhelmingly young. Customs data show more than half of

travelers are under age 30 as of 2023  (up from 31% in 2018). This aligns with STP’s population (median age ≈18.6) . Focus groups cite “youth unemployment” and desire for education or work abroad. The peak emigrant age range is roughly 20 –34.

- Household role:  Most migrants are children of household heads. In surveyed

migrant households, migrants were usually sons or daughters . When one parent migrates, the other typically remains. Consequences include “care gaps” for the left -behind generation . - Internal migration:  More than 50% of STP families report at least one internal

mover (often to the capital) . Rural youth also relocate seasonally (e.g., fishermen). However, STP’s internal flows are modest compared to international migration.

subsections.title: Destinations and Origins
subsections.content: São Toméan emigrants concentrate in a few countries. Destinations:  As of 2021, about 51.7% of the diaspora lived in Portugal, 17.2% in Angola, 16.4% in Gabon, with Cabo Verde and Equatorial Guinea at ~4 –5% each [6]. These five countries combined host ~95% of all emigrants [7][6]. (Other destinations, including France and various African or European nations, account for the remaining ~5%.) subsections.title: Migration Types and Status
subsections.content:
- Economic and labor migration:  Virtually all international emigration is economic

or family -related. São Toméan migrants generally depart by plane on legal visas (work, study, reunification). There is no major guest -worker program; many obtain work/residence in Portugal under CPLP term s. Seasonal irregular labor (e.g. fishing) is minimal due to no open borders by sea [22].

- Immigration:  Immigration into STP is very low (2,139 in 2020) [8]. Most

immigrants are from neighboring lusophone countries (Cape Verde, Angola, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) as noted above [23]. There is no formal refugee intake or asylum processing [13]; STP does not grant asylum status.

- Asylum/Refugees:  STP signed the 1951 Refugee Convention but has no domestic

asylum law [14]. UNHCR records show zero  registered refugees or asylum -seekers in STP as of 2021 [24]. Any São Toméans needing protection generally seek it abroad (not within STP).

- Irregular migration:  Cases are negligible. STP’s island geography means nearly all

movements are documented at airports. The only irregular pattern is visa - overstay, and Frontex reports only a single known irregular São Toméan entry into the EU in 15 years [25]. STP is not a significant transit route or trafficking source (TIP reports have no entries).

- Internal displacement:  Internal (internal) migration mainly follows rural→urban

paths. Heavy rains/flooding displaced ~500 people in 2021 [26], but such environmental displacement is rare. There is no large -scale displacement crisis.

subsections.title: Remittances
subsections.content:
- Trends:  Remittance inflows to STP are very small and falling. The World Bank

reports STP received only US$7.7 million in remittances in 2022, down from US$25.2 m in 2014 [9] (a >70% drop). Outflows (money sent abroad by emigrants) grew modestly to US$4.38 m in 2022 [27].

- Net flows:  As of 2023, STP was still a slight net receiver (net +US$3.3 m) [28].

Given GDP ≈US$500 m, remittances contribute only ~1 –2% of GDP. The decline is attributed to weaker economic ties and possibly tighter banking controls [29].

- Per-migrant:  São Toméan migrants remit far less than peers. A 2025 blog notes

São Tomé’s diaspora remits ~US$266 per capita annually, compared to US$1,525 for Cabo Verdeans [10]. (Remittance portal data rank STP’s average cost of sending at ~12%, higher than regional average [30].)

- Channels:  Remittances in STP are mostly informal cash transfers; formal banking

networks are limited. High fees and lack of access mean many rural families rely on visitors or postal services. The costly and irregular nature of transfers likely depresses remittance  volumes [31][9].

- Household impact:  For the poorest households, even small remittances matter

(e.g. for food or school fees). But overall migration to date has yielded scant investment in São Tomé’s economy. Social research finds most remittances are used for immediate consumption in vulner able households [9][32].

subsections.title: Drivers of Migration
subsections.content:
- Economic factors:  By far the largest drivers are economic. STP’s economy was

stagnant (~0% growth in 2022 [33]) and offers few formal jobs. Youth unemployment (~21% in 2023 [11]) and underemployment push young people to seek work abroad. Focus groups cited “high food prices and low wages” as key push factors [12]. Two -thirds of São Toméans are under 35 [11], creating high job competition.

- Social and educational factors:  Education opportunities motivate migration.

Limited tertiary education on the islands means many students study abroad and stay on. Language/cultural ties to Portugal (colonial legacy) and CPLP channels serve as pull factors. Portuguese consular data show  many family and student visa applications to Europe.

- Environmental factors:  STP is vulnerable to climate (cyclones, sea -level rise) but

so far migration for environmental reasons is minimal. The notable event was floods in mid -2021 (500 people displaced) [26]. Some agricultural decline (e.g. cocoa shocks) may indirectly push families to diversify through migration, but no large -scale climate -driven migration has been documented yet.

- Political context:  São Tomé has been politically stable (no conflict -driven

diaspora). The main political influences on migration have been policy changes, e.g. Angola’s 2000s labor pacts and the 2022 CPLP visa -free agreement [15]. There was also minor political unrest in the 1990s -2000s, but not on a scale to create refugees. timeline title Key Migration Events (2020 –2025) 2020 : COVID -19 travel restrictions cause ~55% drop in departures [3] 2021 : Diaspora ~18% of population; internal floods displace 500 [7] [26] 2022 : CPLP visa -free mobility pact signed [15] 2023 : Departures exceed pre -COVID levels (+106% vs 2019) [3] 2024 : Preliminary data (Jan –Feb) show continued high outflows [17]

subsections.title: Data Gaps and Resources
subsections.content:
- Coverage:  There are no annual official migration statistics published by the STP

government. Most data come from infrequent surveys or external sources. We rely on the 2020 census -based migration profile [7] and a World Bank 2025 study (using customs and survey data up to 2023) [2][3].

- Recent years:  Data for 2024 –2025 are largely unavailable. We have only early

2024 border data [17]. The diaspora share for 2023 is projected (World Bank) but not from a new census.

- Discrepancies:  Minor inconsistencies exist between sources. For example, the

IOM profile [7] and the World Bank 2025 report [6] give virtually identical distributions for 2020 vs. 2021 (differing by ~0.2 –0.5% in each category). We prioritized the most recent (World Bank 2025) for trend analysis, and used the IOM profile for 2020 baselines.

- Sources checked:  We examined STP’s census, IOM/UN migration profiles, World

Bank data portals, UN DESA (KNOMAD), and major development reports. We found no standalone Portuguese -language official migration statistics beyond census figures. Key data (flows, remittances) co me from World Bank and IMF databases [9][28]. sections.title: Employment Segmentation
sections.content: The labor force is segmented into three primary areas, with a notable shift toward the service sector in recent years, The Main employment sectors are services, agriculture, and tourism.

subsections.title: Sector Breakdown
subsections.content: Sector  Estimated % of Labor Force  Key Activities Services  ~60-65%  Public administration, tourism, retail, and small -scale trade. Agriculture  ~15-20%  Cocoa (the main export), coffee, palm oil, and subsistence fishing. Industry  ~15-19%  Construction, light manufacturing (textiles, soap, beer), and energy.

subsections.title: Labor Indicators
subsections.content:
- Unemployment Rate:  Currently hovering around 9.2%.

- Youth Unemployment (15 –24): Relatively stable compared to regional neighbors

at approximately 8.6%, though underemployment remains a challenge.

- Informal Econom y: A significant portion (estimated over 40%) of workers are

self-employed or work in the informal sector, often in street vending or artisanal fishing.

- Gender:  The labor force is nearly evenly split by gender (approx. 49.7% female),

though women are more frequently found in the informal trade and service sectors.

subsections.title: Cost Of Living
subsections.content:
- Wages and Salaries by Sector:  To combat inflation, the statutory minimum

wage was increased to 3,000 STN (approximately $123 USD) per month as of October 2025.1 Salaries vary significantly by sector: public sector professionals typically earn between €400 and €800 per month, tourism and hospitality workers earn between €300 and €600, and agricultural workers earn the lowest formal wages at around €200 to €400.2

- Cost of Living and Daily Expenses:  Because the island imports most of its

manufactured goods and food, living expenses can be high.3 A 3-bedroom city apartment costs around $650 per month, monthly utilities for a family are about $70, and basic groceries range from $250 to $300. Dining out at a local restaurant generally costs between €10 and €20 for a meal.

- Labor Market and the Informal Economy:  The island faces a severe

unemployment crisis, with a national rate of 15.7%.4 This disproportionately affects youth (21.3%) and women (14.6%).4 Consequently, many residents are forced into the "informal sector" (unregistered daily labor or street retail), which is quite large and accounts for roughly 28.7% of the GDP, leaving many workers with unstable incomes and no social safety nets.5 Minimum Wage in Sao Tome and Principe for 2026 - Remote People, accessed March 19, 2026, https://remotepeople.com/countries/sao -tome -and- principe/employer -of-record/minimum -wage/ Work in São Tomé and Príncipe - VisitWorld.Today, accessed March 19, 2026, https://visitworld.today/sao -tome -and-principe/work/info Sao Tome and Principe | Economic Indicators | Moody's Analytics - Economy.com, accessed March 19, 2026, https://www.economy.com/sao -tome -and- principe/indicators São Tomé and Príncipe Economic Outlook, accessed March 19, 2026, https://www.afdb.org/en/countries -southern -africa -republic -sao-tome -and- principe/sao -tome -and-principe -economic -outlook São Tomé and Príncipe - ISS African Futures, accessed March 19, 2026, https://futures.issafrica.org/geographic/countries/sao -tome -and-principe/ Sao Tome and Principe graduates from least developed country ..., accessed March 19, 2026, https://unctad.org/news/sao -tome -and-principe -graduates -least - developed -country -status

subsections.title: System Structure, Access and Enrollment
subsections.content:
The system follows a 6 -3-3 model & Portuguese is the language of instruction at all levels

- 6 years of compulsory primary (ages 6 –11)

- 3 years of lower secondary

- 3 years of upper secondary

Primary enrollment is very high (95% –98%) One of the highest rates in Sub -Saharan Africa & Only about 70% complete primary school whereas Less than 60% transition to lower secondary

subsections.title: Literacy, Enrollment & Key Demographics
subsections.content: Adult literacy rose from 74.9% a decade ago to 93% by 2023, driven by the Quality Education for All Project since 2014, which boosted teacher training and infrastructure. Youth (15 -24) literacy nears universality, though 2% have no formal education and 36% incomplete primary, per older EPDC data.
